2176: The English grammar a programmer needs, by topic: parts of speech, tenses, sentence structure, verbs with special rules, punctuation, common mistakes by Arabic speakers, and clear writing. Each rule has an explanation, a wrong example and a right one, with a grammar quiz at the end.
2183: Some verbs take -ing after them: avoid, finish, suggest, consider, keep. Others take to: want, need, decide, plan.
2185: since + a starting point (since 2023, since Monday). for + a length of time (for two years). Both usually go with the present perfect.
2187: will for a decision made now or a promise. going to for a plan decided before. There is no to after will.
2188: Present continuous for work in progress
2189: am/is/are + -ing for something you are doing now.
2190: who for people, which or that for things. Don't repeat the pronoun after them.
2192: because, so, but, however (followed by a comma), although, therefore.
2194: -er for short words (faster), more for long words (more reliable). Never use both.
2196: too + adjective = more than needed. adjective + enough = sufficient. enough comes after the adjective.
2198: Write languages and tools the official way: Python, JavaScript, GitHub, n8n, macOS. A sentence and the word I always start with a capital.
2201: Plural without an apostrophe: APIs, URLs, PRs. The 's is only for possession.
2203: Put a space between the number and the unit (5 MB, 30 seconds), and use a plural noun with any number except 1.
2205: said without a person after it (He said that…). told needs a person after it (He told me that…).
2207: Most nouns add -s. Nouns ending in s, x, ch or sh add -es. Consonant + y becomes -ies.
2209: Some nouns have irregular plurals: person → people, child → children, index → indices or indexes, analysis → analyses.
2211: I, he, she, we and they are subjects (before the verb). Me, him, her, us and them are objects (after a verb or preposition).
2212: After prepositions (between, for, with, to) use the object pronoun: me, not I.
2214: my, your and our go before a noun (my laptop). mine, yours and ours stand alone (it's mine).
2216: Use myself, yourself and itself when the subject and object are the same, or for emphasis. Don't use them instead of me.
2218: With several adjectives: opinion → size → age → shape → colour → origin → material → purpose, then the noun.
2220: -ed describes how you feel (I'm bored); -ing describes what causes the feeling (the meeting is boring).
2222: good is an adjective for nouns (good code). well is an adverb for verbs (it works well). feel well = healthy.
2224: Most adverbs are adjective + -ly: quick → quickly, careful → carefully. An adverb describes the verb, not the noun.
2226: always, usually, often and never go before a normal verb and after to be: I always test / it is always slow.
2228: many with countable nouns (many bugs), much with uncountable nouns (much time). a lot of works with both.
2230: a few with countable (a few files), a little with uncountable (a little memory). Without a, the meaning is "not enough".
2232: some in positive sentences and offers; any in negatives and questions (Are there any errors?).
2233: Each and every take a singular noun
2234: each and every take a singular noun and a singular verb: every user has a role.
2236: After one of the, the noun is plural, but the verb is singular because the subject is one.
2238: the + -est for short words (the fastest), the most for long words (the most secure). Irregular: good → better → best, bad → worse → worst.
2239: Prepositions of time: in / on / at
2240: at for clock times, on for days and dates, in for months, years and parts of the day.
2242: in = inside (in the folder), on = on a surface or page (on the page, on GitHub), at = a point or address (at the office).
2243: was/were + -ing for an action in progress in the past, often interrupted by another action.
2244: have/has been + -ing for something that started in the past and is still going on, often with for and since.
2245: had + past participle for something that happened before another past event.
2247: With a finished time (yesterday, last week, in 2024) use the past simple. With no time, or up to now, use the present perfect.
2248: Verbs not used in the continuous
2249: State verbs like know, understand, need, want, belong and mean are not normally used with -ing.
2251: Many verbs don't use -ed: write-wrote-written, run-ran-run, build-built-built, send-sent-sent, break-broke-broken.
2252: No will after when and if
2253: After when, if, as soon as and before, use the present tense for the future, not will.
2255: used to + verb for a past habit that stopped. Question and negative: did you use to / didn't use to.
2257: In past questions and negatives, did carries the past, so the main verb returns to its base form.
2259: With does and doesn't, the verb has no -s.
2261: An English sentence starts with the subject, then the verb, then the object; time and place come at the end.
2263: there is + singular or uncountable, there are + plural. Use it to say that something exists.
2264: The verb agrees with the real subject, not the nearest noun: The list of users is empty.
2266: everyone, everybody, nobody and someone take a singular verb.
2268: Don't use two negatives in one sentence (don't + nothing). Use anything or any.
2270: Answer with the same auxiliary: Does it work? Yes, it does. / Is it ready? No, it isn't.
2272: After Can you tell me / Do you know, use normal word order without do/does.
2274: When you report past speech, the tense usually moves back: "I am busy" → He said he was busy.
2276: If + present, present: for something that always happens, like code behaviour.
2278: If + past, would + verb: for an unreal or unlikely situation now.
2280: If + had + past participle, would have + past participle: for something that did not happen.
2282: Past: was/were + V3. Present perfect: has been + V3. Future: will be + V3.
2284: Items in a list should have the same form: all -ing, all verbs, or all nouns.
2286: Don't join two full sentences with only a comma. Use a period, and/but/so, or a semicolon.
2288: A sentence needs a subject and a verb and a complete idea. "Because…" alone is not a sentence.
2290: An opening phrase must describe the subject that comes right after it.
2292: let + person + verb without to (let me check). allow + person + to + verb (allow users to log in).
2294: must when you think it is necessary; have to for an outside rule. Negatives differ: don't have to = not necessary, mustn't = not allowed.
2295: Can, could and be able to
2296: can for ability now, could for past ability or polite requests, will be able to for the future.
2297: would like + to + verb or a noun; it is more polite than want.
2298: to here is a preposition, so it is followed by -ing.
2299: A verb after a preposition takes -ing
2300: Any verb after a preposition (before, after, by, without, for, about) takes -ing.
2302: explain something to someone. There is no "explain me".
2304: discuss, contact, enter, reach, answer and ask take the object directly.
2306: depend on, consist of, interested in, good at, responsible for, agree with, wait for, listen to.
2308: lie = to rest or be located (no object). lay = to put something down (has an object). The past of lie is lay.
2310: Instead of a direct command: Could you…? / Would you mind + -ing? / Please + verb.
2311: After would you mind use -ing; agree with "No, not at all."
2313: Some phrasal verbs can take the object in the middle (turn it off). A pronoun object must go in the middle.
2315: Separate list items with commas. The comma before the final and (Oxford comma) is optional but clearer.
2317: Put a comma after However, For example, Unfortunately and In my opinion at the start of a sentence.
2319: When and or but joins two full sentences, put a comma before it.
2321: It joins two complete, related sentences without and; the next word starts with a small letter.
2323: Before a list, an explanation or an example, after a complete sentence.
2325: 's for singular (the user's email), s' for plurals ending in s (the users' emails).
2327: it's = it is or it has. its = belonging to it (no apostrophe).
2328: For exact words, a message or a button name. In American English, periods and commas go inside the quotes.
2330: When two words describe a noun together before it, join them with a hyphen: a well-known tool, a two-step process.
2332: Days, months, languages, nationalities and companies start with a capital: Monday, March, English, Egyptian.
2334: Use them rarely in formal emails, and only one at a time.
2336: US: May 3, 2026. UK: 3 May 2026. At work ISO is clearest: 2026-05-03. Time: 3:30 PM.
2338: In normal writing: write one to nine as words and 10 or more as digits. Don't start a sentence with a digit.
2340: Don't forget the verb to be
2341: Arabic can drop the verb ("the server down"). English needs is/are/am.
2343: When you talk about something in general, don't use the: Security is important.
2345: Arabic often repeats the subject ("the manager he said"). English uses the subject once.
2346: The adjective comes before the noun
2347: Arabic says "file big"; English says "big file". Adjectives are never plural: new files.
2349: In a question the auxiliary comes before the subject. Arabic often asks with tone only.
2350: Not "from" for time up to now
2351: Arabic says "I work here from two years". English: I have worked here for two years.
2353: also and even go before a normal verb and after to be, not at the start like Arabic "kaman".
2354: p and b, v and f
2355: Arabic has no p or v, so they often become b and f: say problem, not "broblem"; very, not "fery".
2356: Fixed phrases: the same as, different from
2357: the same as (not the same like), different from, similar to, compared to.
2359: return back, repeat again, free gift, future plans: the second word adds nothing.
2361: could've sounds like "could of", but it is written could have / should have / would have.
2363: a lot is always two words. allow (permit) is a different word.
2365: fewer with countable nouns (fewer errors), less with uncountable nouns (less memory).
2367: who is the subject (who wrote this?), whom is the object (to whom did you send it?). In speech, who is fine for both.
2370: In emails and reports, say who did what: We fixed the bug. Use the passive only when the doer does not matter.
2372: Remove very, really, basically, in order to and at this point in time.
2374: If a sentence has and more than twice, split it into two.
2376: A client does not need code details; a developer does. Decide who will read it before you write.

2380: Choose one and stay consistent: color/colour, organize/organise, center/centre. Tech docs are usually American.
2382: farther for physical distance, further for degree (more): further details.
2384: feel good = happy or satisfied. feel well = healthy.
2385: The plural of issue is issues.
2386: The plural of person is people.
2387: The subject form is I, and the other person comes first.
2388: After the preposition to, use me.
